unit.title: Perform advanced manual thermal cutting, gouging and shaping

summary: This unit takes your thermal cutting beyond straight lines. You will learn to plan and mark out work to a tolerance, and to cut shapes, holes, bevels, pipe and sections with oxy-fuel and plasma, using guides, templates, radius bars and trolleys. You will also learn to gouge with oxy-fuel, air carbon arc and plasma, to back-gouge joints and remove faulty welds, and to check, finish and report on the work, safely at every step.

blocks.p: Thermal cutting uses heat to cut and shape metal. You may already cut straight lines by hand with an oxy-fuel torch. This unit is the **advanced** step: cutting to a tolerance; cutting shapes, holes, bevels and pipe with guides and templates; and **gouging**, which removes metal to make a groove, take out a faulty weld or prepare the back of a joint for welding.

Fabricators in Jamaica use these skills every day: cutting base plates and gussets for steel buildings, bevelling plate and pipe for welding, cutting holes for pipes and bolts, removing cracked welds from truck bodies, trailers and farm machinery, and taking down old steelwork at wharves, factories and farms.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres who can already set up an oxy-fuel outfit and make straight cuts.

Shut down and report
Close the equipment down safely, clean up, record results and report faults.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on safety, equipment, planning, bevels, holes, shapes, thick and thin plate, pipe, gouging processes, cut quality and finishing.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: cutting a 30° bevel with a root face, a hole with a radius bar and a shape round a template in 12 mm plate with an oxy-acetylene torch; and gouging a groove and removing a fillet weld by air carbon arc gouging. The assessor watches your set-up, safety and checking as well as the finished parts.

blocks.note: Learn the trade words in the Revision section: kerf, drag, dross, root face, witness line, stack cutting, washing, back gouging, consumables and transferred arc. Short-answer questions ask for them exactly.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Advanced cutting and gouging put out more heat, more molten metal and, with the arc processes, more light, noise and fume than straight cutting. Plan the safety of every job before you light up or strike an arc.

blocks.label: Remember

ul: Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn fiercely. Clothing that has soaked up oxygen catches fire from a spark and burns hard.
**Never** use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or the bench, to cool yourself, to "freshen" the air in a tank or to drive air tools.
Never let oil or grease touch an oxygen regulator, valve or fitting: oil and oxygen under pressure can catch fire on their own.
Never cut a drum, tank or pipe that has held fuel, oil or chemicals until a competent person has cleaned and tested it and said it is safe.

blocks.note: Much cutting is done outside the workshop: on wharves, at factories, on farms and in yards. Before you start, get the hot-work permit if the site uses one; clear dry grass and bush (especially in the dry season), rubbish and fuel; find out what is on the other side of walls and under floors; and keep LPG cylinders well away. Keep a fire watch after you finish, for at least 30 minutes or longer if the site's rules say so.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Anyone with a heart pacemaker or other implanted device must get medical advice before working with, or close to, plasma or arc gouging equipment.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: How the processes work and choosing one

blocks.p: An oxy-fuel cut is a **chemical** cut. The **preheat flames** heat the steel to its ignition (kindling) temperature, a bright red heat of roughly 870–900 °C. A jet of pure **cutting oxygen** then makes the hot iron burn (oxidise) very quickly, and the force of the jet blows the molten oxide, the **slag**, out of the cut. The steel is not melted through: it is burned away in a narrow slot called the **kerf**.

So oxy-fuel cuts only **carbon and low-alloy steels**. For the cut to work, the metal must ignite before it melts, and its oxide must melt at a lower temperature than the metal so that it runs out of the cut. Stainless steel and aluminium make oxides that melt far above the metal and block the cut, and cast iron melts before it will burn. These metals are cut with plasma or mechanically.

A plasma torch passes a gas (in most workshop machines, clean compressed air) through a small nozzle together with an electric arc. The arc heats the gas so much that it becomes **plasma**: an extremely hot, fast jet that conducts electricity. A **pilot arc** starts inside the torch; when the torch is close to the work, the arc jumps to the work and becomes the **transferred arc** that cuts. The plasma melts a narrow kerf and the gas jet blows the molten metal away. Because it melts the metal rather than burning it, plasma cuts **any metal that conducts electricity**, including stainless steel, aluminium and galvanised sheet.

Air carbon arc gouging melts the metal with an arc between a **carbon electrode** and the work, and a strong jet of **compressed air** blows the molten metal out of the groove. It does not depend on the metal burning, so it works on most metals, including stainless steel and cast iron.

blocks.label: Remember

ul: A **backfire** is a sharp pop as the flame goes out or snaps back into the nozzle. Common causes: the nozzle touching the work, an overheated nozzle, a dirty or loose nozzle, or too little gas flow. Shut the torch off, find and fix the cause (clean, tighten or cool the nozzle; check the pressures), then relight with the spark lighter.

A **sustained backfire** burns inside the torch with a squealing or hissing sound, and the torch gets hot. Close the torch valves at once (many makers say oxygen first), let the torch cool, and report it.

A **flashback** is a flame travelling back up the hoses towards the regulators. Close the cylinder valves at once if it is safe, keep clear, raise the alarm and report it. The flashback arrestors must then be checked or replaced as the maker says.

blocks.note: A cutting-oxygen lever that sticks, a torch valve that will not close, a leaking hose or a damaged arrestor: shut the gases off, tag the equipment DO NOT USE, and report it. Never oil a sticking lever or tie it down with wire.

Consumables wear as a set. Change the nozzle when its hole is worn oval or enlarged, and the electrode when its centre is pitted deeply, as the maker says; many people change both together.

blocks.note: On most plasma torches the gas swirls so that the squarer edge of the cut is on the **right** of the direction of travel. So cut clockwise round the outside of a part and anticlockwise round a hole, to keep the good edge on the part. Check the maker's guidance for your torch.

sections.title: Planning and marking out for accurate cutting

ul: Read the drawing for the shape, every size, the **tolerance**, the material and its thickness, and any bevels, holes or slots.
Check the plate: right grade and thickness (measure it), flat, and clean along the cut line. Heavy rust, scale, paint and oil slow the start, spoil the cut face and give off fumes.
Choose the process, the nozzle or current, and the guides you will use: straight edge, cutting trolley, radius bar or template.
Plan where each part will come from on the plate so that waste is small and every cut can be reached.

blocks.p: The **kerf** is the slot of metal removed by the cut. Oxy-fuel kerfs are often about 1.5–3 mm wide on plate up to 25 mm, and plasma kerfs about 1–2.5 mm; a trial cut shows the real width for your settings. Always cut on the **waste side** of the line, so the kerf comes out of the waste and the part stays full size. With a guide, set it so that the edge of the kerf, not the centre of the nozzle, runs along the line: the nozzle centre runs about half a kerf into the waste.

ul: Mark from a **datum**: a straight, square edge or a centre line.
Use a scriber, or soapstone sharpened to a fine edge. A thick line can hide 2 mm.
Centre punch the centres of holes and radii **deeply**, so a radius bar's pivot cannot slip out.
Light centre-punch marks along a cut line stay visible through the scale and the goggles when a scribed line burns away.
Scribe a **witness line** a set distance (for example 10 mm) inside the cut line, on the part. After cutting, check that the distance from the witness line to the cut edge is the same all along.
Mark the waste side of every line, so the cut is made on the right side.
Cut **holes and inside shapes first**, while the plate round them is still whole and stiff. Cut the outside of the part last.
Start every cut in the **waste**: pierce in the waste or run in from the edge of the waste, then turn onto the line.
Leave small **tabs** (bridges) uncut on long, narrow parts and on parts that could move or drop, then cut them last.
Cut long strips with two torches together, one on each edge, so that both edges heat and shrink at the same time.
Support the plate on the cutting table so the part cannot drop, tilt or close the kerf onto the torch as it comes free.

blocks.p: The cut edge gets very hot and expands while the rest of the plate stays cool. As it cools it **shrinks** and pulls, so long narrow strips bow, plates bend and shapes move. Stresses locked into the plate when it was rolled can also be released by the cut. The more heat, and the narrower the part, the worse the distortion.

blocks.p: Before you cut the job, make a short **trial cut on a scrap of the same plate**. It proves the flame or current, the speed and the kerf width, and shows the cut quality before any good material is used.

sections.title: Cutting bevels, holes, shapes, pipe and sections

blocks.h: Straight and bevel cuts with a guide

ul: Clamp a straight edge (a length of angle iron works well) so the nozzle runs along the line, or set up a cutting trolley on its rail. The guide holds the **height, angle and line** steady along the whole cut, which a free hand cannot do.
For a bevel, tilt the nozzle **from the vertical by the bevel angle**: 30° for a 30° bevel. Two plates with 30° bevels make a 60° included angle. Check the tilt with a protractor before you start.
A common pipe bevel is 37.5°, giving a 75° included angle.
Keep the speed steady and do not stop part-way: every stop leaves a notch in the face.

blocks.h: Where to mark a bevel line

blocks.p: A bevel cut from the top face comes out of the edge above the bottom face, leaving the **root face**. The line on the top face is set back from the edge by the depth of the bevel × tan (bevel angle).

**Example:** 10 mm plate, 30° bevel, 1.5 mm root face. The bevel is 10 − 1.5 = 8.5 mm deep, and tan 30° is about 0.577, so mark the line 8.5 × 0.577 ≈ **4.9 mm** in from the edge. The root face can also be left a little bigger and ground to size afterwards.

blocks.h: Circles and holes with a radius bar

When the jet is through, bring the nozzle upright, move out to the line and put the pivot point in the punch mark
Cut steadily round, keeping the bar flat on the plate
Watch where the slug or disc will drop: keep feet and hoses clear

ul: Make the template from steel sheet stiff enough not to buckle, and check its size against the drawing first.
The nozzle runs a set distance off the template's edge, so the template must be made smaller or larger than the part by that distance plus half the kerf.
Clamp the template firmly (or hold it with magnets) and keep the nozzle the same distance off it all the way round, using a spacer or roller guide if you have one.
Never press the nozzle against the template: it damages both.

blocks.p: Several thin plates clamped **tightly** together can be cut as one thick plate: a fast way to cut many identical parts with a good edge. Any gap between the sheets stops the cut, because the oxygen jet loses its force crossing the gap and the next sheet is not hot enough to burn.

ul: Mark a square line round the pipe with a wraparound (a strip of flexible card or thin steel) and soapstone or a scriber.
Support the pipe on vee blocks or a stand at a comfortable height, chocked so it cannot roll, with the waste end overhanging so it falls clear.

blocks.p: **Washing** removes bolt heads, rivet heads and old welds flush with the surface without cutting into the plate. Heat the head, then apply the oxygen with the nozzle (a washing or gouging nozzle is best) held at a **low angle**, almost along the surface, so the head is burned off level with the plate. Punch out the rest of the bolt or rivet afterwards.
**Gouging** removes metal to form a groove: to take out a faulty or cracked weld, to back-gouge the root of a joint, to prepare a groove for welding, or to remove a temporary attachment.
A **gouging nozzle** is curved, and its large cutting-oxygen hole gives a softer, low-speed stream of oxygen, so it burns out a groove instead of cutting through.

flow: Hold the nozzle at a steep angle to preheat the start of the groove to bright red
Open the gouging oxygen gradually while lowering the nozzle towards the plate
Move forward steadily, keeping the stream in the groove
Control the groove: a steeper angle or slower travel makes it deeper; a flatter angle or faster travel makes it shallower; a bigger nozzle makes it wider

head: Equipment
Points to know
rows: Power source
A constant-current (CC) machine able to give high currents. For steel with standard copper-coated electrodes, use **DC electrode positive (DCEP)**.
Gouging torch
Grips the electrode in jaws with air holes, and has a valve to turn the air on and off
Electrodes
Carbon rods coated with **copper**, which helps them carry the current and makes them last longer. The diameter mainly sets the width of the groove.
Compressed air
Clean and dry, at the pressure and flow the maker gives (often about 5.5–7 bar, 80–100 psi)
Current
High: often about 150–400 A for the 4–6 mm electrodes common in training; use the electrode maker's chart

flow: Set up screens, clear anything that can burn, and place the work so the molten metal will blow away from people, hoses and cylinders
Put on full PPE: helmet with a dark filter (about shade 12), ear plugs and muffs, leather gloves, jacket and boots
Fix the work clamp on clean metal near the job and set the current
Fit the electrode with the air holes **below it**, between the electrode and the work, and a short stick-out within the maker's limits
Turn the air on **before** striking the arc, and keep it on
Touch the electrode lightly on the work to strike, without drawing it back
Hold a push angle of about 35–45° and travel steadily forward, so the molten metal is blown ahead out of the groove
Move the electrode forward in the jaws as it burns, to keep the stick-out short
For a deep groove, make several passes rather than one deep one

ul: **Depth** is set by the angle and the travel speed: a steeper angle or slower travel gives a deeper groove; faster travel at the same angle gives a shallower one.
**Width** is set mainly by the electrode diameter: the groove is usually about 3 mm wider than the electrode.
A gouged surface carries a thin **carbon-rich skin**, and can pick up copper from the electrode. Both can make the new weld crack, so **grind the groove back to clean, bright metal** before welding.

Changing angle or speed; unsteady hand
Brace yourself; keep the angle and speed steady

Stick-out too long, or the current too high for the size
Shorten the stick-out; check the current against the chart

blocks.p: **Plasma gouging** uses a plasma torch fitted with gouging consumables, held at a **low angle** to the plate. The current, angle, stand-off and speed set the groove's depth and width. It is cleaner and quieter than arc gouging and easy to control, so it suits lighter work and stainless steel, but it still needs a dark filter, extraction and full PPE.

When a butt joint is welded from both sides, the root of the first side often holds slag, oxide and unfused metal. Before the second side is welded, the root is **back-gouged** from the other side until sound weld metal shows, then ground into a smooth U-shaped groove. The second side can then fuse into clean, sound metal right through the joint.

blocks.h: Removing a crack or a faulty weld

flow: Clean the weld and find the full extent of the fault: find **both ends** of a crack, using dye penetrant if the Centre has it
Mark the area to be removed, a little beyond each end
Get permission and set up safely: screens, fire precautions, PPE
Gouge in **shallow passes**, starting a little before one end and finishing a little past the other
Check the groove often: cracks can run deeper than they look
Grind the groove to clean, bright metal, as a **smooth U shape with gently sloping ends** that the welder can fuse into
Check again (dye penetrant if available) to prove the fault has gone
Preheat if the procedure says, re-weld to the procedure, and inspect the repair

ul: To remove a **fillet weld**, gouge along the weld at a shallow angle in several passes, stopping short of the plate surface, then grind off what is left. Deep gouges in the plate are themselves faults.
To remove a temporary lug or cleat, cut it off a few millimetres above the surface, then grind flush. Never gouge or cut into the parent plate.

blocks.h: What a good cut looks like

ul: A square, smooth face with **fine, nearly vertical drag lines**
A **sharp top edge**, not melted or rounded
Little **dross** (oxide and metal stuck to the underside), which chips off easily
No notches, and sizes within the tolerance

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Kerf
The slot of metal removed by the cut
Drag
How far the bottom of the cut lags behind the top; small drag is good, heavy drag means travel is too fast
Dross
Oxide and re-solidified metal stuck to the bottom edge of the cut
Notch (gouge mark)
A deep step or hollow in the cut face; it can start a crack and must be removed
Top-edge rounding
A melted, beaded top edge

head: Fault
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Top edge melted and rounded, with beads of metal
Preheat flame too strong
Nozzle too close
Travel too slow
Correct nozzle and flame; correct height; faster travel
Heavy dross on the bottom edge
Travel too slow (or so fast the dross is hard and sticks)
Oxygen pressure too low; dirty nozzle
Correct speed and pressure; clean the nozzle
Drag lines curving well back; cut lost at the bottom
Travel too fast
Slow down
Notches or gouges in the face
Stopping and restarting badly
Unsteady hand or travel too fast
Scale or dirt; backfires
Use a guide; clean plate; steady speed; grind out the notches
Face bevelled or not square when it should be
Nozzle tilted
Damaged nozzle bore
Guide set wrongly
Square the nozzle; clean or replace it; reset the guide
Wide, rough kerf
Nozzle too big or too high; oxygen pressure too high
Use the chart settings
Hard, cracked cut edge
High-carbon or alloy steel cut cold and cooled fast
Preheat before cutting as the procedure says; cool slowly; grind off the hard layer

head: Fault

Cure
rows: Heavy, bubbly dross that knocks off easily (low-speed dross)
Travel too slow, or current too high for the thickness
Speed up, or reduce the current
A small, hard bead of dross that is hard to remove (high-speed dross)
Travel too fast
Slow down
Bevelled face; more bevel on one side
Worn nozzle or electrode

Cutting with the poor side on the part
New consumables; correct height and angle; reverse the direction
Arc will not start or keeps going out
Work clamp on dirty metal
Torch too high
Worn consumables; low air pressure
Clean the clamp point; correct height; check consumables and air
Consumables wearing out fast
Wet or oily air
Piercing too close
Running the arc off the edge
Drain and filter the air; raise the torch to pierce; release at the edge

head: Feature
Check with
rows: Lengths, widths and positions
Tape, steel rule, vernier caliper for small sizes
Squareness of edges and faces
Engineer's square

Bevel protractor or weld gauge

Steel rule or vernier caliper
Hole size and roundness
Vernier caliper or rule across several diameters
Shape
The template, and the witness lines
Groove depth and width
Depth gauge or the caliper's depth rod; rule

blocks.p: **Tolerance example:** a part drawn 450 ± 1.5 mm must measure between **448.5 mm and 451.5 mm**. A tolerance of ±2 mm allows a total of 4 mm between the largest and smallest sizes.

ul: Chip off the dross and slag, wearing safety glasses.
Grind the edge to the line, but **not undersize**. Grind small notches out smoothly; deep ones may be built up with weld and ground, if the procedure allows.
Take the sharp edges off corners so the parts are safe to handle.
Grind bevels to clean, bright metal before they are welded.
A part that is out of tolerance is labelled, set aside and reported, never hidden.

blocks.note: When grinding, wear safety glasses and a face shield, check that the disc is the right type, undamaged and rated for the grinder's speed, keep the guard on, and hold the grinder with both hands.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Oxy-fuel:** shut down in the correct order, drain the hoses and release the regulators (see the oxy-fuel section).
**Plasma:** release the trigger and let the post-flow air cool the torch before switching off; drain the water trap; coil the leads.
**Arc gouging:** switch the power off and close the air; put hot stubs in a **metal container**.
Leave hot work to cool in a safe place, marked HOT. Empty the slag tray when it is cold. Sweep up, and keep the fire watch.
Record your measurements on the results card or job sheet.
Report at once any fault (a sticking lever, a leak, a damaged hose, arrestor or cable, worn consumables), any flashback, near miss or injury, and any part that is out of tolerance.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of cutting and gouging and say how each one is controlled, including the right filter shade.
I can explain how oxy-fuel, plasma and air carbon arc processes work, and choose the right one for a job.
I can explain the differences between acetylene and propane.
I can set up, leak test, light, adjust and shut down an oxy-fuel cutting outfit, and say what to do after a backfire or flashback.
I can set up a plasma cutter, check its consumables and air, and cut at the right stand-off and speed.
I can read a drawing, mark out from a datum, allow for the kerf and mark witness lines.
I can plan the order of cuts and control distortion.
I can cut straight lines and bevels with a guide or trolley, and work out where to mark a bevel line.
I can set a radius bar for a hole or a disc, pierce safely and cut a circle.
I can cut round a template, stack cut, and cut thick plate, thin sheet, pipe and sections.
I can wash off bolt and rivet heads.
I can gouge with oxy-fuel, air carbon arc and plasma, and control the depth and width of the groove.
I can back-gouge a joint and remove a crack or a faulty weld ready for re-welding.
I can name cut and gouge faults, with their causes and cures.
I can check cut parts against the drawing and tolerance, finish them, and report the results.

terms: Air carbon arc gouging
Gouging with an arc from a carbon electrode, with compressed air to blow the molten metal away
Back gouging
Gouging the root of a joint from the second side, to reach sound metal before welding that side
Backfire
A pop as the flame goes out or snaps back into the nozzle
Bevel
An edge cut at an angle to prepare it for welding
Consumables
The plasma torch parts that wear out and are changed: electrode, swirl ring, nozzle and cap
Cutting attachment
The part fitted to a welding torch handle so that it can be used for cutting
Drag
How far the bottom of a cut lags behind the top
Dross
Oxide and metal stuck to the bottom edge of a cut
Flashback
A flame travelling back through the hoses towards the regulators and cylinders
Flashback arrestor
A device on each regulator outlet that stops a flashback reaching the regulator and cylinder
Gouging
Removing metal to form a groove
Hot-work permit
Written permission for cutting, welding or other hot work in a place where it could start a fire
Kerf
The slot of metal removed by a cut
Kindling temperature
The temperature, a bright red heat, at which steel will burn in a stream of oxygen
Neutral flame
A flame with equal amounts of fuel gas and oxygen; the normal preheat flame
Piercing
Starting a cut away from the edge by burning a hole through the plate
Plasma
Gas heated by an arc until it is extremely hot and conducts electricity
Radius bar
A guide that holds the torch at a set distance from a centre, for cutting circles
Root face
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevelled edge; also called the land
Stack cutting
Cutting several thin plates, clamped tightly together, in one pass
Stand-off
The distance between a plasma torch and the work
Transferred arc
The plasma arc that passes from the torch to the work and makes the cut
Washing
Burning off bolt or rivet heads flush with the surface, with the oxygen at a low angle
Witness line
A line marked a set distance from the cut line, used to check the cut afterwards

c1.title: Bevelled plates for a water main in Yallahs
c1.text: Damion is cutting plates for a repair sleeve on a large steel water main near Yallahs, St Thomas. Each plate is 10 mm mild steel and must be 600 mm ± 1.5 mm long, with a 30° bevel and a 1.5 mm root face along one long edge. He is using an oxy-acetylene cutting torch on a cutting trolley that runs along a straight rail.

c2.title: Flange rings for a pumping station in Runaway Bay
c2.text: Shavar must cut eight flange rings from 16 mm mild steel plate for a pumping station near Runaway Bay, St Ann. Each ring is Ø300 mm outside with a Ø160 mm hole in the middle, both ±1.5 mm. He is using an oxy-acetylene torch with a radius bar, and his trial cut shows a kerf about 2 mm wide.

c3.title: A cracked weld on a quarry truck in Hayes
c3.text: At a repair shop in Hayes, Clarendon, Akeem must remove a cracked fillet weld about 200 mm long from the 12 mm hinge plate of a quarry truck's tipping body, so it can be re-welded. He is using air carbon arc gouging with a 400 A DC machine, 6.4 mm copper-coated electrodes and the shop's compressed-air line. The truck stands just outside the shop door.

c4.title: Stainless-steel tables for a hotel kitchen in Discovery Bay
c4.text: Annakay is cutting 3 mm stainless-steel sheet for work tables and splash-backs for a hotel kitchen in Discovery Bay, St Ann. She is using a 40 A hand plasma cutter with a drag shield, fed from the shop's compressor. The shop is humid, and the compressor's water trap has not been drained for a week.

c5.title: Taking down an old wharf shed in Kingston
c5.text: Marlon leads a small crew taking down an old steel shed on the Kingston waterfront. The purlins and columns are covered in many coats of old paint, and the column bases are held by large bolts. The crew is using oxy-propane torches, the site has a hot-work permit system, and there is a cable pit beside one of the columns.

questions.q: How far in from the edge should Damion mark the bevel line on the top face of each plate?
o: About 5.8 mm
About 4.9 mm
About 8.5 mm
About 2.9 mm
questions.why: The bevel is 10 − 1.5 = 8.5 mm deep, and the set-back is 8.5 × tan 30° (about 0.577) ≈ 4.9 mm. Using the full 10 mm thickness gives 5.8 mm, which leaves no root face.

questions.q: Damion's first bevel has a rounded, melted top edge with small beads of metal along it. What is the most likely cause?
o: The cutting oxygen pressure was too low for 10 mm plate
The trolley was set to travel much too fast for the plate
The nozzle was tilted the wrong way for a 30° bevel
The preheat flame was too strong or the nozzle too close
questions.why: Too much preheat, a nozzle held too close or travel that is too slow melts the top edge before the oxygen cuts it. Travel that is too fast shows as heavy, curving drag lines instead.

questions.q: A finished plate measures 601.8 mm long. What should Damion do with it?
o: Grind it back to within 600 ± 1.5 mm and measure again
Accept it, as 1.8 mm is close enough to the tolerance
Scrap it and cut a replacement plate from new stock
Report it to the supervisor as faulty steel from the supplier
questions.why: The limits are 598.5–601.5 mm, so the plate is 0.3 mm too long. A part that is long can be trimmed back and measured again; a part that is short is set aside and reported.

questions.q: Before lighting up, Damion sees that the oxygen regulator has no flashback arrestor on its outlet. What should he do?
o: Carry on, as only the fuel-gas side needs an arrestor
Carry on, but keep the oxygen pressure low for the job
Fit arrestors to both regulators before using the outfit
Fit an extra check valve at the torch end of the oxygen hose
questions.why: Flashback arrestors are needed on both the oxygen and the fuel-gas regulator outlets, because a flashback can travel up either hose. Check valves at the torch do a different job and do not stop a flame.

questions.q: With a 2 mm kerf, what should Shavar set on the radius bar for the hole and for the outside of each ring?
o: 81 mm for the hole and 149 mm for the outside
80 mm for the hole and 150 mm for the outside
79 mm for the hole and 151 mm for the outside
78 mm for the hole and 152 mm for the outside
questions.why: The kerf must come out of the waste: for the hole the nozzle runs half a kerf inside the line (80 − 1 = 79 mm), and for the outside of the ring half a kerf outside it (150 + 1 = 151 mm). Setting the plain radius makes the hole 2 mm oversize and the ring 2 mm undersize.

questions.q: Which circle of each ring should Shavar cut first?
o: The Ø300 outside, so the ring is free to handle
The Ø160 hole, while the plate is still stiff
Either, as the order makes no difference to size
Half of each circle, then the other halves in turn
questions.why: Inside shapes are cut first, while the plate round them is still whole, stiff and held. Cut the outside first and the ring is loose and heat-distorted when the hole is cut, and the pivot has nothing firm to sit in.

questions.q: Halfway round a hole, the torch backfires with a loud pop and the flame goes out. What should Shavar do?
o: Turn the gas pressures up and relight straight away
Relight it at once from the red-hot plate and carry on
Change to a bigger nozzle, since 16 mm is too thick
Shut off, check and clean the nozzle, then relight
questions.why: A backfire usually means the nozzle touched the work, overheated, or is dirty or loose. Shut the torch off, put the cause right, and relight with the spark lighter; never relight from hot metal.

questions.q: As Akeem gouges, black, sooty spots of carbon keep appearing in the groove. What is the most likely cause?
o: The electrode is dipping in, or the air is off or weak
The current is set much too high for a 6.4 mm electrode
The work clamp has been fixed too close to the groove
He is gouging on DC electrode positive, as it is set
questions.why: Carbon is left behind when the electrode dips into the pool or when the air is not blowing the metal clear. Turn the air on before striking, keep it on, and hold a short arc without touching the work.

questions.q: The truck stands just outside the door, with its diesel tank on the side Akeem is working from. Which precaution matters most before he starts?
o: Point the molten stream away from the tank, with screens
Wear a darker filter so the molten stream can be seen well
Gouge faster than usual so less molten metal is thrown out
Wet the ground under the truck so the sparks go out quickly
questions.why: Arc gouging blows a stream of molten metal several metres. It must be pointed away from fuel, hoses, cylinders and people, with screens, a clear area, an extinguisher and a fire watch.

questions.q: Akeem's electrode glows red a long way back from its tip and burns away fast. What is the most likely cause?
o: The air pressure is set much too high
The air holes are under the electrode
The stick-out from the jaws is too long
The work clamp is on clean, bright metal
questions.why: A long stick-out carries the high current through too much carbon, so it overheats and burns away; the air jet is also too far from the arc. Move the electrode forward in the jaws to keep the stick-out short.

questions.q: What shape should Akeem leave the groove in before the hinge plate is re-welded?
o: A sharp V with square ends, just as deep as the crack
A smooth U with gently sloping ends, ground to bright metal
A flat-bottomed slot cut right through the hinge plate's thickness
Just as it was gouged, with its skin left on to protect it
questions.why: A smooth U with sloping ends lets the welder fuse into the bottom and the ends of the groove. Grinding removes the carbon-rich skin and copper pick-up that would make the new weld crack.

questions.q: Annakay's cuts have heavy, bubbly dross on the underside that knocks off easily. What should she change?
o: Travel faster along the cut
Travel more slowly along the cut
Raise the torch well off the sheet
Fit a shield of a larger size
questions.why: Heavy, bubbly dross that comes off easily is low-speed dross: she is moving too slowly for the current. Too fast gives a small, hard bead that is difficult to remove.

questions.q: What problem will the undrained water trap cause?
o: The arc will be too hot, and the cut will be too wide for a 3 mm sheet
Wet air will wear the consumables quickly and spoil the cut quality
Water in the air will cool the sheet and stop it distorting
The compressor will run faster and give more pressure
questions.why: Moisture and oil in the air attack the electrode and nozzle and make the arc unstable, so the cut gets worse and the consumables are used up fast. In humid weather the trap needs draining often.

questions.q: What extra fume hazard comes from cutting stainless steel?
o: Zinc fume that causes metal fume fever
Lead fume from the coating on the sheet
Acetylene fume left over from the cut
Chromium and nickel in the fume
questions.why: Stainless steel contains chromium and nickel, which come off in the fume and are harmful to breathe. Use extraction close to the cut and the respirator your instructor gives you.

questions.q: When should Annakay change the nozzle and electrode?
o: Every morning before work, whether or not they are worn
Only once the arc will no longer start at all, even on new sheet
When the nozzle hole is worn oval or the electrode is pitted
Whenever the shield gets dirty with spatter from the cut
questions.why: Worn consumables give a bevelled, dirty cut and can damage the torch, so they are changed when they show wear, as the maker describes. Waiting until the arc fails spoils many cuts first.

questions.q: The purlins have thick layers of old paint. What should be done before they are cut?
o: Strip it back from the cut lines and use extraction
Burn the paint off with the preheat flame first
Cut straight through, as paint fume is harmless outdoors
Wet the paint with water so that it will not burn
questions.why: Old paint may contain lead, and burning paint gives off harmful fume. Strip it back from each cut line, use extraction or work where the wind carries the fume away, and wear the respirator provided.

questions.q: A propane hose has a small leak at a fitting close to the cable pit. Why is this especially dangerous?
o: Propane is lighter than air and rises past the torch flame
Propane is heavier than air and can collect in the pit
Propane leaks only become dangerous when the cylinder is full
Propane makes the cutting oxygen burn more slowly
questions.why: Propane sinks and collects in pits, drains and other low places, where a spark can ignite it long after the leak began. Shut off the gas, find the leak with leak-detection solution and fix it before going on.

questions.q: A crew member starts to blow dust off his overalls with the torch's oxygen. What should Marlon do?
o: Let him, as long as the torch flame is turned off
Let him, as oxygen does not burn by itself
Stop him: oxygen-soaked clothing burns fiercely
Tell him to use the fuel-gas hose for that instead
questions.why: Oxygen trapped in clothing makes it catch fire from a single spark and burn violently. Never use oxygen, or fuel gas, to blow dust off clothing, to cool yourself or to ventilate a space.

questions.q: Natalie must cut a strip 25 mm wide and 1.2 m long from 10 mm plate, and keep it as straight as possible. Which method is best?
o: Cut one edge at a slow speed, then cool it before the other
Cut it with a bigger nozzle so the cut is over more quickly
Cut each edge in short bursts, from both ends towards the middle
Cut both edges at the same time with two torches
questions.why: Two torches heat and shrink both edges together, so their pulls balance and the strip stays straight. Cutting one edge at a time lets the first edge pull the strip into a bow.

questions.q: While stack-cutting four 3 mm sheets, the cut goes through the top sheet but stops at the second. What is the most likely cause?
o: The nozzle is far too large for 3 mm sheet
The sheets are of different grades of steel
The travel speed is too slow for the stack
There is a gap between the first two sheets
questions.why: Stack cutting works only when the sheets are clamped tightly with no gaps. Across a gap the oxygen jet loses its force and the next sheet is not hot enough to burn.
